https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-07-24/w.text: Explore the ABC White House will not fight Tate brothers extradition to UK Topic: Courts Posted Fri 24 Jul 2026 at 10:14am Fri 24 Jul 2026 at 10:14am Fri 24 Jul 2026 at 10:14am Andrew Tate and his brother appeared in a US federal court earlier this week. ( AP: Vadim Ghirda ) In short: Andrew and Tristan Tate are facing extradition to the United Kingdom on rape and sex trafficking charges after their arrest in Miami last weekend. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt says the Trump administration is not planning to intervene in the extradition process. The Tate brothers are avid supporters of US President Donald Trump and were part of the hyper-masculine "manosphere" that contributed to his 2024 election victory. abc.net.au/news/white-house-will-not-fight-tate-brothers-extradition-to-uk/106952928 Link copied Share Share article US President Donald Trump will not stop the extradition of influencer Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan to Britain on sex crime charges, the White House says. Self-professed misogynist Andrew Tate and his younger sibling were detained by US authorities in Miami on Saturday, local time, in a move their lawyer called "politically motivated". The Tates are challenging their extradition. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt was asked at a news briefing if Mr Trump or the administration planned to intervene in the extradition process, and told reporters "no". Tate brothers fight extradition to UK Andrew and Tristan Tate's attorney says an attempt to extradite the brothers is politically motivated. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also distanced the administration from the case. "There's no role for us to play at this moment or maybe ever in that regard," he told reporters in the Philippines earlier this week. The Tate brothers are avid supporters of Mr Trump and were part of the hyper-masculine "manosphere" that contributed to his 2024 election victory. Andrew Tate also tried to cultivate relationships in the past with Mr Trump's sons Don Jr and Barron, US media reported. The Tates were arrested after British prosecutors announced new charges of rape, sex trafficking and assault . They now face 59 charges in total — 42 against Andrew and 17 against Tristan. Their lawyer said on Monday that they were innocent and would fight extradition. Loading... "It's politically motivated. There's no question about it," Joseph McBride told reporters outside a Miami court after a hearing on the case . In Romania, where they have been based in recent years, the brothers face allegations of trafficking minors, sexual intercourse with a minor and money laundering. In March 2025, the US state of Florida launched a criminal investigation into the pair. The status of that investigation is unclear. Congresswoman Yassamin Ansari, a Democrat from Arizona, called for a probe into whether Trump administration officials, congressional offices or people close to Mr Trump improperly intervened to protect the Tates. "No individual — regardless of wealth, political party, or access to the first family and the president — is above the law or beyond the reach of justice," she wrote in a letter to House Oversight Chairman James Comer. https://www.laois-nationalist.ie/news/po.text: Wed, 12 Aug, 2026 - 20:56 Popular Laois priest to leave parish Fr Vard will take personal leave of absence with effect from Friday, 18 September Fr David Vard is taking personal leave from his role as parish priest of Stradbally. File image       Carmel Hayes POPULAR Laois priest Fr David Vard will say farewell to his parish next month, amid major clerical changes announced today. After less than a year as parish priest of Stradbally, Fr Vard will take personal leave of absence with effect from Friday, 18 September. Meanwhile, also popular but somewhat older Fr Tom Dooley is to retire as parish priest of Portarlington and Emo, while curate Fr Ciprian Matei will leave Portlaoise and return to his native Romania. The imminent changes were announced on Wednesday, 12 August by Bishop Denis Nulty of the Kildare & Leighlin diocese, as he confirmed a number of retirements, departures and new appointments. At a time of rapidly declining vocations and a severe shortage of priests, Bishop Nulty said he has been in contact with a number of international priests whom he hopes will be in a position to take up appointments in the diocese. No time frame has been given for Fr Vard’s temporary personal leave but his departure will be widely regarded as a major loss to the parish of Stradbally, which also takes in Timahoe and Vicarstown. He was officially appointed parish priest last October, having spent two years as parish administrator. He quickly became the life and soul of the community, organising the first Stradbally Parish Picnic and getting involved in countless groups and causes, including the Timahoe Male Choir. He even did a group skydive at 10,000 feet to raise funds for new sound systems for all three churches in Stradbally, Vicarstown and Timahoe. He is also remembered for a powerful interview on T he Tommy Tiernan Show on RTÉ television, during his early years in the priesthood. A native of Newbridge, Co Kildare, Fr Vard became the youngest priest in Ireland when he was ordained in June 2017 at the age of 25. He was ordained in his hometown by Bishop Nulty and was immediately appointed curate in Portlaoise parish. He was greatly missed in Portlaoise when he moved to Stradbally in August 2023 to become parish administrator. In Portarlington and Emo, Fr Dooley will be replaced as parish priest by Fr Pat Hughes, who is currently parish priest of Myshall and Clonegal in Co Carlow, while curate Fr Eugen Dragas Tamas will return to the Diocese of Iasi in Romania. Fr Piotr Jakubiak, who serves as Polish Chaplain, will also become a curate in the Portarlington-Mountmellick pastoral area while continuing his work supporting the Polish community. Announcing the diocesan moves, Bishop Nulty said: “These changes are challenging on all fronts, and I cannot express enough how grateful I am for the cooperation, generosity and understanding from all our clergy. “With a big reduction in the number of priests available this year, I am reminded of just how much each priest gives of himself when appointed to a parish. “This is never taken for granted and we should always be thankful for their work and ministry. “Clergy who are moving and those who are taking on more, have my deepest respect and support. “Going forward parishes will undoubtedly be without a resident priest and so with fewer clergy it is more important than ever to pray for our priests and to encourage vocations. “I am in contact with a number of international priests who hopefully will be in a position to take up appointments in the diocese over the coming months. “I ask you to keep all our priests and deacons in your prayers, to help them and to support them at this important time in our diocese. The changes come into effect on Friday, 18 September next.” The changes announced today are: PORTARLINGTON AND EMO • Fr. Tom Dooley, PP Portarlington and Emo to retire • Fr. Eugen Dragas Tamas, CC, Portarlington and Emo returning to Iasi Diocese in Romania • Fr. Pat Hughes, PP, Myshall and Clonegal, to become PP of Portarlington and Emo • Fr. Piotr Jakubiak, Polish Chaplain, to become CC in the Portarlington/ Mountmellick Pastoral Area, while continuing to support the Polish community PORTLAOISE • Fr. Erik Ebot, SVD CC, Portlaoise, recalled by the SVD Order • Fr. Ciprian Matei, CC, Portlaoise returning to Bucharest Archdiocese in Romania • Fr. Petru Medves, CC, Abbeyleix, Ballinakill & Raheen, to become also CC, Portlaoise. The three curates in Portlaoise (Fr. Adriano de Oliveira, Fr. Simon Jin and Fr. Petru Medves) will assist in ministry in the wider Pastoral Area STRADBALLY • Fr. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2e0.text: Figure caption, Watch: Moment two planes fly less than 50 feet above stadium By Damian Zane Â and Â Pumza Fihlani ,Â Reporting from Johannesburg Published 3 hours ago The South African airline behind a daring aerial stunt last Saturday that saw two planes flying in close formation low over a packed stadium has pulled out of doing a similar operation this weekend, the country's aviation regulator, SACAA, has said. Airlink's flying feat divided opinion with some labelling the startling manoeuvre reckless, while others praised the precision and expertise on display. SACAA said that while it had approved the applications and safety measures for the flybys, it was now investigating further following "discussions in the media". Airlink has not commented on the reported cancellation of Saturday's display that had been due to place over a stadium in Soweto. Footage of last weekend's air show before the start of a rugby match in Cape Town, featuring fierce rivals South Africa and New Zealand, was shared around the world. The flight tracking website Flightradar24 said that according to its analysis "the lead aircraft passed less than 50ft (15m) above the top of the stadium". From some angles the jets appeared very close to the roof of the DHL Stadium as they roared over amid coloured flare smoke. Image source, Gallo Images/Getty Images Image caption, The planes - one green, one black - flew over the stadium shortly before the start of the South Africa-New Zealand match The airline said the flights were performed with the "approved and rehearsed safety altitude and speed limits for the flypast" and were conducted by a "highly experienced crew". But Airlink will not be repeating the flights over the stadium in Soweto, Johannesburg, that is hosting the third and deciding test between the Springboks and the All Blacks, according to SACAA. The regulator said that while the company had followed all the correct procedures it had now "obtained the flight data recording downloads as well as other additional requirements" for further analysis. "SACAA, as the safety net of the South African skies, gives the public the assurance that aviation safety and security compliance will always remain paramount and is not negotiable," it said in a statement emphasising the excellent air safety record in the country. The flyby has been a feature at major sporting and presidential events in South Africa several times over the years - using both military jets and commercial airlines. https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-c.text: Europe war-games life after Merz The German chancellor's foes at home are rejoicing at his political downturn. But those in Brussels aren't. By GABRIEL GAVIN and FRIDA PREUß Illustration by Natália Delgado/ POLITICO The EU can't pretend Friedrich Merz isn't in trouble any longer. After a string of humiliating election losses where the far right has made historic gains and an internal fight with his own coalition over social care policy, EU partners are starting to plan for the prospect that the German chancellor could be ousted — or at least distracted — in the crucial coming months, according to five diplomats and officials who spoke to POLITICO. They were granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive talks. Two European governments have even held internal sessions to game out what the end of Merz’s chancellorship would mean for EU policymaking, two of those familiar with the discussions said. Advertisement Advertisement It's not a prospect they take lightly. Merz leads the EU’s largest economy and is the chief negotiator for wealthy countries seeking to rein in spending in the bloc’s proposed €2 trillion seven-year budget. He is also a driving force behind EU efforts to save heavy industry. "Any debate about the German chancellor weakens Germany's role in the EU and in the world," said Wilhelm Gebhard, a member of the Bundestag and an official in Merz's governing CDU party. With France facing its own far-right surge and a presidential election next year that could hand power to euroskeptic Marine Le Pen, few in Brussels relish the prospect of Germany, historically the EU's other major player, turning inwards or derailing important negotiations. The contingency planning, which has seen officials and diplomats brainstorm the situation, comes after months of mixed signals from Berlin on EU policy, including car emissions and a proposed social media ban for children. Even if Merz stays in office, the political turmoil is already complicating Berlin’s work on the EU’s biggest files. The worst-case scenario for Brussels would be a leaderless Germany, or one with a far-right government. But that is seen as virtually impossible in the short term, with none of the mainstream players seeking new elections while the far-right Alternative for Germany party are leading in the polls. “All coalition partners know that they have a great deal to lose from early elections,” said Hannah Neumann, an opposition Green MEP who sits on the European Parliament’s security and foreign affairs committees. “My expectation, therefore, is that they will stay together and muddle through.” Advertisement Advertisement While Merz himself could be forced to resign in the face of his growing unpopularity, he would be replaced straight away by a successor from either his center-right CDU party or his center-left coalition partner, the SPD. That should give Brussels confidence "someone will always be in charge," said one of the diplomats. GERMANY NATIONAL PARLIAMENT POLL OF POLLS All 3 Years 2 Years 1 Year 6 Months Smooth Kalman For more polling data from across Europe visit POLITICO Poll of Polls . Searching for a win Those who know him insist Merz won't be distracted when it comes to EU affairs. "Other politicians might say 'OK, I focus less on EU politics.' For him it’s just the opposite: It’s an additional incentive to show leadership in Europe,” said a person familiar with the chancellor’s thinking. In the immediate term, Merz's political weakness at home could make finding compromise on the bloc’s next seven-year budget harder by pushing the chancellor to double down on Berlin’s hardline stance in search of a win, a further two diplomats warned. As the leading voice for countries seeking a smaller EU budget, which leaders hope to agree by year-end, Merz has called for cuts of “hundreds of billions of euros.” Germany, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Austria and the Netherlands are pressing for overall reductions, while net recipients such as Poland and Romania want to protect their share. Nobody who could replace him as chancellor "would be able to be more flexible than Merz is," said one of the diplomats, but "the risk is he has to show his self-perceived leadership in Brussels in the hope it will help his standing in Germany." Advertisement Advertisement An envoy from another country said "domestically he is weak [which means] he can't compromise" and needs to be seen to score a win by slashing the budget as far as possible. But Merz's allies say his fight on the world stage is only worthwhile if his coalition partners play along behind the curtain. "Strength comes not just from grand appearances in Brussels, but above all from stability, reliability and the ability to push through decisions at home. That is precisely what is lacking at the moment," said CDU Bundestag member Fabian Gramling. "Germany's influence in Europe also depends on how united and capable of action the federal government appears at home." Friedrich Merz is pictured during a meeting with soldiers in Münster, Germany on Oct. 1, 2026. | Hesham Elsherif/Getty Images Infighting and indecision The fractious relationship between the CDU and the SPD has already been undercutting Berlin's stance on issues of critical national importance. Throughout 2025, as Brussels renegotiated a planned phaseout of combustion engine cars, in the face of fierce lobbying from Germany's influential automotive sector, German officials and diplomats were unable to articulate a clear position, with center-right ministers wanting to scrap the green policy and their center-left counterparts pushing to preserve it. Ultimately Merz's fellow German conservatives in Brussels — Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European People's Party chief Manfred Weber — stepped in to kill the proposal at the eleventh hour. Advertisement Advertisement Another key policy area where the coalition struggled to agree a position was on whether children should be banned from social media, a flagship EU-wide proposal from von der Leyen. While Merz personally backed the idea at the start of the year, he and his political allies spent more than six months struggling to land on a specific age limit to lobby for when von der Leyen was consulting with partners, according to officials and diplomats involved in the talks. Even before the latest crisis, Merz’s domestic troubles were spilling into Brussels at the highest level. Last year, he surprised fellow EU leaders by demanding that a summit scheduled to cover geopolitics and other policy files should instead focus on saving European heavy industry from competition with the U.S. and China. Germany lost around 124,100 industrial jobs last year, according to an analysis by EY , with the government concerned deindustrialization is helping drive support for Merz’s far-right and far-left rivals. Other capitals share his concerns, but Merz has insisted industry should top the agenda at future summits. But even inside the chancellor's own CDU, he has struggled to achieve consensus on what to do about it. As the Commission plans a push against unfair Chinese trade practices, Merz's fellow party member and foreign minister Katherina Reiche is seen as more protective over the relationship with Beijing, and the German industrial giants like Volkswagen and BASF that trade with it. In a speech on Thursday commemorating 36 years of German reunification — the fall of the Berlin Wall and the dissolution of communist East Germany —the country's ambassador to the EU, Thomas Ossowski, told fellow envoys and officials that "whenever we celebrate German unity, we celebrate European unity. And we need this unity [now] more than ever." Gabriel Gavin reported from Brussels. Frida Preuß reported from Berlin. Jordyn Dahl, Eliza Gkristi and Carlo Martuscelli contributed to this report. But a warming planet is making these changes more frequent: in a population skewed towards one sex, individuals may run out of mates to reproduce with Updated - October 12, 2026 11:05 am IST - BENGALURU Rupsy Khurana READ LATER SEE ALL Remove An agile frog, 2017. As temperatures continue to climb, scientists are asking whether increased sex reversal could affect the long-term survival of amphibian populations. | Photo Credit: Petar Milošević (CC BY-SA) Some fish can switch sex more than once over a lifetime. In lizards, genetically male hatchlings can be born looking and functioning as females. In some frogs, genetically female individuals can develop into fertile males. This phenomenon is called sex reversal . It is well documented in the animal kingdom, from invertebrates to amphibians to birds, where an individual can begin life with one sex and later switch to another. But a warming planet is making these changes more frequent and potentially more consequential for animals. In a population skewed towards one sex, individuals may run out of mates to reproduce with, slowing population growth, reducing genetic diversity, and ultimately raising the risk of extinction. Invasive species may be the wrong enemy in a changing subcontinent Agile frogs Around 40% of amphibian species face the risk of extinction, which makes them the most threatened vertebrates on the earth. As temperatures continue to climb, scientists are asking whether increased sex reversal could affect the long-term survival of amphibian populations. To answer this, a group of researchers turned to agile frogs in Hungary. They found that sex-reversed wild males sire fewer offspring — which are in turn more vulnerable to heat and infectious disease. These disadvantages could together speed up population declines as the planet keeps warming. The results were published in Science Advances on September 3. In agile frogs as in mammals, the sex at birth is determined by chromosomes. Two X chromosomes make a genetic female whereas an X and a Y make a genetic male. But excessive heat in the tadpole stage can override that genetic recipe and turn some genetically female tadpoles into physically normal and fertile male tadpoles. “Theoretical models suggest that this threat can be mitigated, up to a certain severity of climate change, for example XX males siring all-XX offspring,” said Veronika Bokony, the study’s lead author and researcher at the HUN-REN Centre for Agricultural Research. However, “this mitigating effect can be lost if sex-reversed individuals cannot participate in reproduction.” Young cold-blooded animals are suffering the most as Earth heats up, research finds Chance of mating Bokony et al . first looked at whether animals whose sex differs from their genetic sex reproduce just as successfully in the wild. They paired 20 sex-reversed males with 20 sex-concordant males, matched for body size and arrival time at the breeding ponds, two traits known to affect mating success. They let each male mate with a female. The team then tracked whether the female laid eggs, how long it took, and whether the eggs developed into tadpoles. The team found that sex-reversed males were just as capable of winning mates and fertilised eggs did develop into tadpoles. However, sex-reversed males did not have an equal chance at mating. About one-third of females paired with sex-reversed males laid only part of their eggs, called the split clutch strategy in which they saved the rest for a better mate. In an experimental set-up, females had no choice, so sex-reversed males could still coerce the female into mating and sire a clutch. “Had they been free in a real mating aggregation, this could have allowed the female to find another male who could replace the sex-reversed male by fighting,” Dr. Bokony said. Science for All | Scientists find bacteria living on fish brains Artificial heatwave So the researchers turned to breeding ponds in the wild. They sampled more than a hundred egg masses from 16 different populations and found that even though the sex-reversed male agile frogs made up roughly 20% of the wild populations, only 4% of egg clutches belonged to them. “This suggests that when the frogs mate freely, the sex-reversed individuals are not as successful at becoming sires as the sex-concordant males,” Dr. Bokony said. The few offspring they did sire were also not in the clear. As researchers tracked the development of lab-reared tadpoles, they found that 61% of the offspring of sex-reversed males underwent sex reversal, developing as males despite being genetically female. Only 17% of offspring of sex-concordant males did, however. “We were suspicious that sex reversal might have negative consequences on individual fitness and on population viability,” Dr. Bokony said. A warming climate is also amplifying the threat of infectious diseases. The pathogen ranavirus is of particular concern: in some instances, it has wiped out more than 90% of tadpoles in a single event. To understand how well these offspring could withstand such climate-driven stressors, researchers exposed eggs from sex-reversed and sex-concordant males to an artificial heat wave along with ranavirus. Under high temperatures, tadpoles of sex-reversed males carried higher viral loads. With lower paternity, higher rates of sex reversal in offspring, and greater disease susceptibility all being plausible outcomes, the team turned to computer models to test how these combined pressures could affect wild agile frog populations. Climate change pitting humans and wildlife against each other, say Indian conservationists Higher extinction risk “What happens in the laboratory and what occurs in the field are two different matters, and the strength of this study lies in the assessment of the impact of sex reversal in the wild,” University of Canberra professor Arthur Georges, who was not involved in the study, said. Their results showed small populations were especially vulnerable, since losing even a few breeding females could affect a population’s ability to reproduce. While some populations may already have begun declining, others could disappear within 60 to 70 years as heat-driven sex reversal pushed populations towards more males with fewer females to mate with. When the model factored in the mortality from ranavirus among the offspring of sex-reversed males, population decline began roughly 10 years earlier and extinction came about 9.5 years sooner. Without ranavirus, populations still declined about eight years earlier — but the extinction occurred only about two years earlier. “We, as scientists, underestimate the number of sex-reversed individuals in populations and species,” Dominique Potvin, associate professor at the University of the Sunshine Coast, Australia, said. She added that scientists need to know how the environment is affecting sex reversal and affecting the long-term survival of species to update their interpretations and management strategies for conservation. Rupsy Khurana is science communication and outreach lead at the National Centre for Biological Science, Bengaluru.
